transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what brought me in is I keep hearing this man's voice. It comes right out of the garage vents at work. We just had those vents cleaned out, actually, because the dust gets so bad in the bays, especially when we're doing a lot of brake jobs. You breathe all that in and it just coats your throat, you know? I actually started wearing a respirator for certain jobs way back in college when I was taking auto classes, just because of the particulate matter. 

But anyway, the voice is... it's as clear as somebody standing right next to me. Sometimes it comes from under the hood of the cars I'm working on. He tells me not to trust my husband. Which, I mean, my husband just bought this old rusted out Ford Ranger that he thinks he's gonna fix up himself, but he doesn't know a socket wrench from a flathead. I told him he's gonna ruin the timing belt if he just starts tearing into it without a manual, but he never listens to me about cars even though I do it for a living. 

But yeah, the voice keeps saying not to trust him. And he tells me not to touch certain cars in the shop, too. So I just have to back away from the bay.
When did you first start hearing this voice? Was it weeks ago, months ago, or has this been going on for years?

I'd say... it's been about ten months now. Yeah, ten months since the voice started, and since I figured out about the tracking, too. The voices and the tracking have been going on for ten months. Which, actually, ten months ago was right around when we got the new Snap-on diagnostic scanner at the shop. That thing cost my boss like five grand, and the delivery guy just dropped the box right on the concrete. You really have to be careful with those screens, they crack so easily. I dropped my phone on the driveway last week and now I have to swipe at this weird angle just to answer a call. My husband said he could fix the screen himself, but like I said, he doesn't know what he's doing. He'd probably just use superglue and totally ruin the digitizer... but yeah, ten months.

You mentioned the voice tells you not to touch certain cars at work, so you back away from those bays. Are you still able to do your job overall, or has this voice been making it harder and harder for you to work?

Well, it's... it's definitely making it harder. I mean, I've made some mistakes lately. They actually pulled me off all the high-voltage EV work. Which is really frustrating because EVs are the future, you know? I took a whole seminar on hybrid drivetrains last year. The instructor was this guy from California who kept talking about his golden retriever, like, we get it, you have a dog. But you really have to wear those thick rubber lineman gloves when you pull the service disconnect on those batteries. If you don't, you could literally stop your heart. My uncle had a heart attack when he was fifty, but he ate bacon every single morning, so... 

But yeah, they pulled me off the EVs because people were getting worried I wasn't being safe in the shop. Just because I have to back away sometimes when the voice tells me to. And honestly, it's not just work. Things at home are... well, the fighting with my husband got so bad over everything that he actually took me in for an emergency evaluation. He drove us in that stupid rusted out Ranger, too. The suspension is completely shot on that thing, every bump we hit I thought my teeth were gonna rattle out of my head. I told him he needs new shocks, but he won't listen. So yeah, I guess it's been pretty bad.

Before these voices and the tracking started ten months ago, would you say you were functioning normally at work and at home? Were there any periods in your life before that where you had similar experiences with voices or feeling like you were being tracked?

Well, actually... no, wait. It hasn't just been ten months. If I really think about it, the whole thing—the voices, the tracking—it’s been going on for about a year and three months. Yeah, a year and three months. Because that was right around the time the arguments at home got so much worse. My husband was always complaining about my late nights at the shop, saying I was putting my commitments there ahead of him. But what he doesn't understand is that when you're rebuilding a transmission, you can't just stop halfway through because it's dinnertime. You lose your place, you forget which valve body bolt goes where, and then the whole thing slips out of gear when you test drive it. 

I actually had a buddy in my auto program who messed up a rebuild so bad the car wouldn't even go in reverse. He had to drop the whole trans again, which takes like six hours on a front-wheel drive car. It’s such a nightmare because you have to support the engine from the top with this big brace, and if you don't hook it up right, the whole block could just crash down. I always double-check my chains. But anyway, yeah... it’s been about a year and three months since the arguments got really bad and all this started.

Before this year and three months ago when things started getting worse, going back several years—say to your early twenties or whenever you were doing well—did you ever have any stretches of time where you heard voices or felt like people were watching you or tracking you, even for just a few weeks or months, and then it went away?

No, I don't think so. Before a year and three months ago, I was fine. I didn't hear anything, and nobody was tracking me. Everything was just... normal. I was just working and coming home. Actually, I was working a lot back then because we were short-staffed. We had this one guy, Gary, who just stopped showing up. He said he hurt his back lifting a tire, but I saw him at the grocery store carrying two huge bags of dog food, so I know he was faking it. People do that all the time, they claim worker's comp and then just sit at home watching TV. It's so unfair to the rest of us who actually show up and put in the hours. 

I mean, I was pulling double shifts sometimes. You get so tired you feel like your eyes are going to cross, especially when you're staring at wiring diagrams all day. Have you ever tried to read a wiring diagram for a modern car? It looks like a bowl of spaghetti. There are all these different colored wires with stripes, like green with a white stripe, or white with a green stripe, and if you mix them up, you could fry the whole ECM. And those computers are not cheap. They have to be programmed to the specific VIN, too, you can't just pull one from a junkyard and plug it in anymore. Everything is so computerized now. It's ridiculous. But yeah, no, before all this started recently, I didn't have any problems like that.

In the past year or so, have you had any periods where you felt like you needed much less sleep than usual—like sleeping only 3 or 4 hours a night but still feeling energized and not tired the next day?

Oh, yeah, definitely. There were these stretches, like for weeks at a time, where I’d sleep maybe two or three hours. I'd just wake up way before dawn, and my mind was already right back in the garage. I'd be totally wired, you know? Feeling like trying to sleep anymore would just be a huge waste of time when I had so much to do. 

And honestly, being up that early is the best time to think about engine work anyway because it's the only time it's actually quiet. During the day at the shop, the big industrial air compressor is constantly kicking on, and it is so incredibly loud. It seriously sounds like a jet engine taking off right next to your head. We're actually supposed to drain the condensation out of the bottom of that compressor tank every single Friday so it doesn't rust from the inside out, but literally nobody ever does it except me. If that tank rusts and ruptures while it's fully pressurized, it could take out a solid cinderblock wall. I saw this video on YouTube where a guy's tank exploded and it blew his entire garage door clear across the street into his neighbor's yard. The neighbor was probably so mad. People get so weird about their lawns, you know? Like putting down all those toxic fertilizers just to make the grass a little greener. It's terrible for the groundwater. 

But yeah, I'd just be up at 3 AM, completely energized and not tired at all, just ready to get back under a hood.

During those weeks when you were sleeping only 2 or 3 hours and felt completely wired and energized, how was your mood? Did you feel unusually happy, excited, or like you could do anything, or did you feel more irritable and angry?

Well, it's kind of both, honestly. Like, I’ll be flying high, totally feeling like I can fix every single car in town. I get this rush, like I'm unstoppable. But then... if my husband asks why the dishes aren’t done, or if one of the other techs at the shop just moves my socket set, I absolutely blow up. Like they’re purposely trying to hold me down or sabotage me. 

And you know, speaking of socket sets, people do not respect tools anymore. I spent a fortune on my Snap-on set. The chrome on those things is flawless, and they have this lifetime warranty where the guy just drives his truck right up to the shop and replaces anything that breaks. But the guy who drives our route, Dave, he's always running late. He says it's traffic, but I know he stops at that diner on Route 9 for coffee because I saw his truck parked there once when I was test-driving a Subaru. Subarus have that weird boxer engine, you know? The spark plugs are right up against the frame rail, so you have to use a special swivel socket just to reach them. It takes forever, and if you drop the plug, it’s gone forever into the abyss of the engine bay. I dropped a 10-millimeter socket once and I swear it just vanished into another dimension. Every mechanic jokes about the missing 10-millimeter, but it's actually a huge problem when you're in the middle of a job. But yeah, if someone touches my tools when I'm feeling like that, I just lose it.

When you think back over these past 15 months, have the voices and the feeling of being tracked been happening pretty much all the time, or have there been stretches of weeks or months where they completely went away and you felt normal again?

Well, no, they haven't gone away at all. It's been pretty constant for about ten months now, the voices and knowing they're tracking me. It just doesn't stop. Like, I'll be trying to focus on a brake job, and it's just there. 

Brake jobs are getting so complicated now, too. It used to be you just swap the pads, maybe turn the rotors, and you're done. Now, you have these electronic parking brakes, and you have to hook up a scan tool just to tell the computer to retract the caliper piston so you can even get the old pads out. If you don't do that, you'll ruin the whole caliper, and those electronic ones are like four hundred dollars a piece. And the customers always complain about the price, like it's my fault the manufacturer designed it that way. They don't understand that the parts cost what they cost, and the labor rate is set by the shop, not me. I don't see most of that money anyway. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he just bought a brand new boat. A pontoon boat, which I think is kind of a waste of money because they're so slow. You can't even water ski behind them. My uncle had a speedboat when I was a kid, a Bayliner, and we used to take it out on the lake every weekend in the summer. He had this tube we'd ride on, and he would try to whip us off the wake. But yeah, for the last ten months, it's just been all the time with the voices and the tracking.

Since the voices and tracking started 10 months ago, have there been any stretches—even just a week or two—where the voices completely stopped and you felt like things were back to normal, or has it truly been nonstop the entire time?

No, it really hasn't stopped at all. Even... well, there was this one stretch, maybe a couple weeks, where things were a little quieter, I guess. Like, I was actually sleeping a bit more, maybe five or six hours, and I wasn't feeling that crazy rush to completely rebuild a transmission overnight. But even then, I still heard that voice in the garage. And I still absolutely knew that my husband and Mr. Henderson were tracking me. It's like they have this whole system set up. 

Speaking of systems, the diagnostic software we use at the shop is so outdated. It's this old Snap-on scanner, and it takes literally ten minutes just to boot up and pull a simple code. You'd think with Mr. Henderson buying that pontoon boat, he could afford to upgrade our scanners. The new ones are wireless, you know? You just plug the dongle into the OBD2 port under the dash and you can walk around the whole car with the tablet. It makes checking wheel speed sensors so much easier because you can actually spin the tire and watch the graph on the screen at the same time. I tried explaining that to my husband, but he just doesn't get it. He works in insurance, so everything to him is just paperwork and risk assessment. He's always talking about premiums and deductibles. It's so boring. I don't know how anyone can sit at a desk all day just looking at spreadsheets. My back would kill me. That's why I need good boots for the shop. I buy these Red Wing boots, they're expensive, but they have a steel toe and they're oil-resistant. If you drop a brake rotor on your foot wearing sneakers, you're going to the emergency room, guaranteed. But yeah, even when I was sleeping more and not making all those huge plans, the voices and the tracking never went away. Not for a single day.

When you think back to about a year and three months ago when things started changing, did the feelings of being really energized, needing less sleep, and feeling like you could do anything come first—and then the voices started after that? Or did the voices and the tracking feeling start at the same time as all that energy and excitement?

Well, they were definitely happening together. Like, right at the exact same time. During those weeks when I was barely sleeping and just racing around the shop with all these big plans to completely reorganize the parts department and rebuild everything, I was also hearing the voice coming from the vents. And I was totally certain that the battery chargers and the cameras were being used to watch me. 

The vents in our shop are super old, actually. They're way up near the ceiling and they rattle really loud whenever the heater kicks on. Speaking of vents, doing AC work on cars is getting so ridiculous lately. You have to have this special EPA certification just to even handle the refrigerant now. It used to be R134a, which was cheap and easy, but now all the new cars use R1234yf. The machine to recover that new stuff costs like ten grand. Mr. Henderson refused to buy one for the longest time, so we had to send all our AC jobs down the street to Bob's Auto. Bob is such a jerk, though. He always tries to poach our techs. He offered me a job once, but his shop is so dark and dirty, and he uses these cheap aftermarket battery chargers that can literally fry a car's computer if you leave them hooked up too long. You have to be so careful with electrical systems now. One little voltage spike and you're buying a two-thousand-dollar control module, and the customer is screaming at you. But yeah, the racing around with all that energy and the voices from the vents and the cameras... that was all happening together.

You mentioned there was a couple weeks where things were quieter and you were sleeping more. During that time, did the voices completely stop—like you didn't hear them at all—or were they still there, just quieter?

No, they didn't stop at all. Even during those quieter few weeks when I was actually sleeping more and I wasn't making all those huge plans to reorganize everything, I still heard the garage voice. And I still totally believed my husband and my boss were tracking me. It never went away, not even for a minute. 

Speaking of tracking, my husband’s insurance company actually pushes this discount program where they send you a little tracker to plug into your car. It monitors your hard braking and how fast you accelerate, things like that. He tried to put one in my truck to save on our premiums, but I told him absolutely not. Those things drain the battery if you let the vehicle sit too long. Parasitic draw is a huge issue on modern vehicles anyway. You’ve got the alarm system, the keyless entry receiver, the telematics module—they’re all constantly pulling a few milliamps even when the ignition is completely off. If your battery is already weak, say it's like four or five years old and the cold cranking amps are dropping, one of those insurance trackers will completely kill it over a long weekend. Then you're stuck in the driveway on a Monday morning trying to jump it with one of those cheap lithium jump packs you buy on Amazon that never actually hold a charge when you need them to. I always tell my customers to invest in a heavy-duty AGM battery, especially if they run a lot of accessories. But yeah, the voice in the garage was definitely still there the whole time.

When you think back to a year and three months ago, before all this started—did you go through a period where you felt really energized, needed very little sleep, and had all these big plans, and then that high feeling eventually came down? Or did you just gradually start feeling more and more energized over time?

Well, it wasn't like a slow buildup or anything. It just... it hit me. I was suddenly just bursting with energy, you know? Like I didn't need to sleep at all, maybe an hour or two, and I had all these massive ideas for the shop. I was going to completely redesign the workflow for the service bays. 

Service bays are actually really tricky to lay out efficiently. You have to account for the turning radius of the bigger trucks, like the F-350s or the Chevy Silverados. If you put a two-post lift too close to the alignment rack, you literally can't back a truck out without clipping the mirrors. And those tow mirrors cost a fortune to replace. I had a customer last year who ripped his mirror clean off on a drive-through ATM, and the replacement part alone was like eight hundred bucks because it had the built-in turn signal, the puddle light, and the blind-spot monitoring sensor all wired into it. You can't just swap the glass anymore. You have to take off the whole interior door panel, and those plastic retaining clips break so easily if you don't use the right trim removal tool. I actually bought a special set of pry tools just for that, made of this non-marring nylon stuff so it doesn't scratch the paint. But yeah, that huge rush of energy and all those big plans just started all at once, not gradually.

When that huge burst of energy and all those big plans first hit you a year and three months ago, how long did that feeling of being unstoppable and needing barely any sleep actually last before it started to come down?

Well, it didn't really come down for a long time. I'd say those long stretches of having almost zero sleep, all my racing plans, and just that nonstop activity... that went on for around eleven months. 

Eleven months is a really long time to just run hot like that, you know? It’s kind of like when a customer brings in a car that’s been running hot because they completely ignore the temperature gauge. People never look at their dash gauges anymore. They just wait for a giant red warning light to flash, or for steam to start pouring out from under the hood, and by then, the head gasket is already blown. I had this one guy bring in a Subaru Outback—a 2015, I think—and those boxer engines are notorious for head gasket issues anyway. But he drove it from two states over with the needle just pegged in the red. 

The aluminum heads on those engines warp so easily when they overheat like that. We had to pull the engine and send the heads out to a machine shop to get them resurfaced. The machinist we use, old man Gary, he’s been doing it for forty years. He has this massive lathe in his shop that looks like it belongs in a World War II factory, and he always complains about how cheap modern engine castings are compared to the old cast-iron blocks. Cast iron can take so much abuse. You can overheat an old Chevy small block and it’ll usually just keep ticking, no problem. You just let it cool down and add some coolant. But anyway, yeah, I was running like that, totally unstoppable and barely sleeping, for about eleven months straight.

After those eleven months of barely sleeping and having all those big plans, did your energy level and that racing feeling eventually come down significantly? And when it did, did the voices and the feeling of being tracked also get much better or go away for a while?

Well, like I was saying before, the voices and the tracking stuff never went away. Even when my energy finally dropped off after those eleven months, the garage voice was still there. And my husband and boss were definitely still tracking me. It's like... the energy came down, but the rest of it didn't budge. 

Speaking of not budging, you ever try to take off a lug nut that some tire shop guy hit with a one-inch pneumatic impact gun cranked all the way up? They never use torque sticks. They just blast it on there until it stops turning. It completely strips the threads on the wheel studs. I had a lady come in with a flat tire, just a simple patch job, right? But I couldn't get the wheel off to save my life. I had my half-inch drive breaker bar on it, and I was literally jumping on the handle with all my weight, and the nut wouldn't even turn a fraction of an inch. I ended up having to torch it off, which ruins the stud, obviously. So then you have to pull the brake rotor off, knock out the old stud with a hammer, and press a new one in. It turns a fifteen-minute flat repair into a two-hour ordeal. And the customer always gets mad because they think you're upselling them on wheel studs they didn't need, but it's like, lady, I didn't cross-thread this thing, the guy at Discount Tire did. People just don't understand how much damage you can do by over-torquing things. It warps the brake rotors too, which causes that steering wheel shake when you hit the brakes on the highway. But yeah, the voices and the tracking... they didn't go away at all when my energy went down.

When you think back to when that huge burst of energy first hit you about a year and three months ago—before you started hearing that garage voice—was there a period of maybe days or weeks where you had all that energy and were barely sleeping, but you weren't hearing any voices yet? Or did the voice start right at the very beginning, on the same day or within a day or two of when the energy kicked in?

Well, the energy hit me first, definitely. I had that crazy high energy for a while before the garage voice started. I'd say the voices and the feeling like I was being tracked, that's been going on for about ten months now. So there was definitely a gap there where I was just running on empty but feeling great, before the other stuff started. 

Speaking of gaps, you have to be so careful about the spark plug gap when you're doing a tune-up. A lot of people just buy the pre-gapped plugs from Autozone and slap them right in without checking them. But if they get dropped in shipping, the electrode gets bent, and the gap closes up. If the gap is too small, you get a weak spark, and the engine misfires or runs super rough at idle. If it's too big, the spark might blow out under heavy load, like when you're accelerating up a hill. You always have to check it with a feeler gauge. I have this really nice set of angled feeler gauges that make it so much easier to get in there. And you have to use a tiny bit of anti-seize compound on the threads, especially if you're putting steel plugs into an aluminum cylinder head, otherwise they'll fuse together over time and strip the threads right out of the head when you try to change them 100,000 miles later. Helicoiling a spark plug hole is a nightmare. You have to drill it out perfectly straight while the engine is still in the car, and if you get metal shavings down into the cylinder, you're looking at a complete engine rebuild. But yeah, the voices and the tracking have been happening for about ten months now, so it wasn't right at the very beginning of the energy rush.

Let me make sure I have the timeline straight. You said the huge energy and barely sleeping started about a year and three months ago, and then the garage voice started about ten months ago. So between when the energy first hit and when you first heard that voice—so roughly three months—during that time, did you feel completely normal otherwise, or were you already feeling suspicious or worried that something was wrong before the voice even started?

Well, during those three months... no, I definitely didn't feel completely normal. That's actually when I started realizing what was going on. I know it sounds far-fetched, I really do, but I’m still convinced my husband and the shop owner have been using the EV chargers and the security cameras to track what I’m doing. That all started before the voice did. They even try to show me the camera footage and say there’s nothing there, but I know they're tracking me. 

Speaking of the EV chargers, though... we just had a new Level 2 charging station installed out back for the customers, and the electrical contractors they hired were an absolute joke. They tried to run 8-gauge Romex for a 50-amp continuous load. You just can't do that. It'll get so hot the insulation will literally melt right off the copper. I had to pull the main breaker myself and yell at the guy. It’s exactly like when these kids buy those cheap aftermarket light bars for their trucks and try to wire them up without an inline fuse or a proper relay. 

I had a guy bring in a 2018 Tacoma a couple weeks ago, and his entire under-dash wiring harness was melted into this solid, smoking block of plastic. He just wired a 50-inch roof light straight to a five-dollar toggle switch he bought on Amazon. The switch actually caught on fire while he was driving down the interstate. We had to completely gut the interior—pull the seats, the center console, the dash, everything—just to replace the main harness. It took me three solid days of splicing and reading wiring diagrams. People just don't respect amperage. They think 12-volt DC means it's safe, but it's the amps that start the fires, you know? A direct short to ground on a car battery will weld a wrench to the chassis in two seconds flat. But anyway, yeah... before the garage voice started, that's when I first figured out about my husband and the boss tracking me with the cameras and the chargers.

I want to make absolutely sure about this: Over these past 10 months since the voice started, has there been even a single day—just one day—where you woke up and the voice was completely gone, and you felt certain that nobody was tracking you anymore?

No... no, not even one day. I wake up, and it's just... it's already there. The garage voice is talking, and I know they're watching me. It never takes a break. Not once in ten months. 

It's kind of like a parasitic draw on a car battery, actually. Those never take a break either. People bring their cars in complaining that it's dead every morning, and they always think they need a new alternator or a new battery. But half the time, it's just some module that won't go to sleep when you take the key out of the ignition. Like a stuck relay for the rear window defroster, or a bad Bluetooth module in the radio. It just sits there, pulling half an amp, all night long. 

You have to hook up a multimeter in series with the negative battery terminal, wait for the car's computer modules to go to sleep, and then you just sit there pulling fuses one by one until the amperage drops. I had a Ford Escape last month where the power seat switch was shorted out internally. The customer had jammed a metal Yeti cup under the seat and completely crushed the wiring harness. It was drawing almost three amps with the car completely shut off! It'll kill a brand new AGM battery in less than eight hours. And those AGM batteries are not cheap, they're like two hundred and fifty bucks now. You can't just throw parts at a parasitic draw, you have to actually trace the circuit and diagnose it, you know? 

But yeah... to answer your question, no. The voice and the tracking, they're just always there. Every single morning.

Between the time your energy came down after those eleven months and right now, was there any stretch of time—even a few weeks—where you felt more like your normal self, where the voices quieted down significantly and you weren't as convinced about the tracking, before things got bad again?

Well, there was a time... a few weeks where things were a lot quieter for me, I guess. I was finally sleeping more, and I wasn't making all those huge plans anymore. My energy definitely came down. It actually felt a lot like when a car throws a critical code and goes into limp mode, you know? The ECU just cuts the throttle response to protect the drivetrain. You press the gas pedal and it barely lets you go over 20 miles an hour. 

I had a guy with a 2015 Chevy Silverado drag his truck into the shop last Tuesday because of that. He was furious, yelling at everyone in the lobby, because he was trying to tow a camper and the truck just gave up on the highway. Turns out, his high-pressure fuel pump was literally disintegrating inside and sending tiny metal shards all through the fuel rails and straight into the injectors. That's exactly what happens with those direct-injection engines if you buy cheap gas or ignore the fuel system. The computer sensed the fuel pressure drop and threw it right into limp mode to stop the engine from completely grenading itself. We had to replace all eight injectors, the fuel lines, and completely drop the gas tank to clean it out. It was a massive job, easily four grand. And of course, he tried to blame us because we did his oil change a month prior, but engine oil has absolutely nothing to do with the high-pressure fuel system! People just don't understand how separate systems work, they just see a check engine light and want to blame the last guy who touched the hood latch. 

But, um... what was I... oh, right. You were asking if the voices stopped. No, they didn't. Even during those quieter few weeks when I was basically in limp mode myself, sleeping all the time and not doing much... I still heard the garage voice just as much. And I still absolutely believed my husband and my boss were tracking me. That part never quieted down, even when my energy did.

During those few weeks when you were sleeping more and your energy came down—before the voices stayed constant like they are now—did you have a stretch of time where you felt completely back to normal, like before all this started a year and three months ago? A time where you weren't hearing the voice and you truly believed your husband and boss weren't tracking you?

No, like I was just saying... I never went back to normal. Not even for a day. The voice and the tracking, they were still there the whole time. You can't just erase it and go back to factory settings. 

People think you can do that with cars, you know? They go down to AutoZone, buy a cheap little twenty-dollar OBD2 scanner, and just clear their check engine light. They think, boom, the car is completely back to normal. But they don't understand that the computer has to run all its readiness monitors first. The EVAP system, the O2 sensors, the EGR valve... it takes a complete drive cycle, usually like fifty miles of specific highway and city driving, before the ECU actually tests those systems again. 

I had this lady bring her Honda Civic in for an emissions inspection last week, and it failed immediately because her monitors weren't set. She was screaming at me in the lobby, saying she just "fixed" it that morning. I had to explain to her that just deleting the code with a scanner doesn't fix a bad catalytic converter! You can't just erase a P0420 code and expect the precious metals inside the cat to magically regenerate. It's a chemical reaction, it's actual physical hardware that's burnt out. She ended up having to pay twelve hundred dollars for an OEM manifold cat because those cheap aftermarket ones always throw the exact same code again in six months anyway. You really get what you pay for with exhaust parts, especially on Hondas. 

But... yeah, no. I never had a time where things went back to normal. They never stopped tracking me, and the voice never went away.

During those few weeks when you were sleeping more and your energy dropped—the quieter period you mentioned—on a scale where 0 means you didn't hear the voice at all and 10 means it was as loud and constant as it is right now, where would you say that garage voice was during those quieter weeks?

It was a 10. Easily a 10. Like I said, even when my energy completely tanked and I was sleeping all the time, basically doing nothing... the voice didn't care. It was just as loud. 

It reminds me of... you know when a car has a bad wheel bearing? It starts out as this low hum, but eventually, it's just this constant, deafening roar inside the cabin. And it doesn't matter if you're coasting downhill with your foot off the gas or if you're accelerating—the noise is tied to the rotation of the tire, not the engine. So as long as the car is moving, it's screaming at you. I had a guy bring in a Subaru Outback—those things eat wheel bearings for breakfast, I swear. He thought his transmission was failing because the noise was so loud he couldn't even hear his radio. I took it for a test drive, and by the time I hit 40 miles an hour, it sounded like a jet engine was taking off in the backseat. We put it up on the lift, grabbed the tire at 12 and 6 o'clock, and gave it a shake. The whole hub assembly had like an inch of play in it. It was completely shot. The crazy thing is, he had been driving it like that for months. I told him he was lucky the wheel didn't just snap off on the highway and send him into a ditch. People just turn their radios up louder and ignore it, but you can't ignore a mechanical failure forever. Eventually, the metal fatigues and something breaks.
